messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Ideas for RStan
parts:
On Jun 6, 2014, at 9:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, Bob. I put it on stan-dev because non R-users might have thoughts too.
Thanks.

> At some point we can talk about how best to write a spec. My main thought is to switch to Sebastian's function (or something like it), also to clean up the stan-optimize call and a few other things.

I don't think we need a formal spec process --- just
a simple functional spec consisting of the documentation for
the functions you want to see implemented including examples.
Then, the folks who know R can turn it into a technical spec
that explains how to implement it, but I don't think we
need to formalize a technical spec if the functional spec is solid.

I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
of examples. Here's what I would like to see for compilation:

model <- compile("foo.stan");

for fitting:

mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);

and for saving and reloading:

save_model(model=, file=);
model <- load_model(file=);

To turn this into a functional spec we can work from,
we have to add descriptions of

* the rest of the arguments

* types for each argument

* return type

* constraints on legal calling patterns --- the spec has to
say exactly what arguments require other arguments or disallow
other arguments, and what sets of legal values there are (this
is the killer that most R functions don't even bother with, making
them very difficult to learn)

* types of errors that get thrown under what conditions

* description of what the function does

* examples of how the function is used in practice

I don't really underestand R well enough to talk about the
types myself or error handling, other than in broad generalities.

You'll see that using primitive functions will make writing
this spec much easier, which will in turn make development and
testing much easier. It should also make it easier to play around
with higher-level functions that may be more changeable and less
well supported (due to prohibitive combinatorics of testing and doc).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Ideas for RStan
parts:
On Friday, June 6, 2014 6:14:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
of examples.  Here's what I would like to see for compilation:

  model <- compile("foo.stan");
Okay, if you are willing to get rid of stan_model(), which does the same thing.

for fitting:

  mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
Using optimize() would be poor choice of a function name because there is already a base function with that name and rstan already has optimizing().
mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);
Okay, or the existing sampling() function

and for saving and reloading:

  save_model(model=, file=);
  model <- load_model(file=);

Still have no earthly idea why we would need save_model() and load_model() when there are already base functions called save() and load() that work for any object, including models produced by stan().

Ben

On Jun 7, 2014, at 1:47 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, June 6, 2014 6:14:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
> of examples. Here's what I would like to see for compilation:
>
> model <- compile("foo.stan");
>
> Okay, if you are willing to get rid of stan_model(), which does the same thing.

I just looked it up, and stan_model's just fine, including
the doc.

>
> for fitting:
>
> mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
>
> Using optimize() would be poor choice of a function name because there is already a base function with that name and rstan already has optimizing().

You're right. Part of this spec should be choosing good names.

I think we should step back and rename a bunch of functions and deprecate
the existing ones. I think functions should be verbs (not gerunds like
"optimizing" or nouns like "stan_model"); I'd also prefer class names
to be nouns ("stanmodel" is good). But if R uses gerunds for functions,
so be it --- I don't want to fight their conventions.

> mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);
>
> Okay, or the existing sampling() function

That's fine. Though I find the doc very confusing because
I don't know what an S4 method is, so my immediate question is
how I call an S4 method. I assume many of our
users won't either, but maybe we just need to tell them (and me)
to go learn R.

I think this means I should just butt out of R design.
I'd like the doc to be something I can understand, but I realize
I may just be too clueless about R to qualify as an RStan user.

> and for saving and reloading:
>
> save_model(model=, file=);
> model <- load_model(file=);
>
> Still have no earthly idea why we would need save_model() and load_model() when there are already base functions called save() and load() that work for any object, including models produced by stan().

That's great! (The earthly idea, though not my intention,
for duplicated function names is discoverability. I didn't think
save() and load() worked for Rcpp objects --- didn't we have a long
discussion about why it's nearly impossible to serialize? Isn't that
why we read the data back into R data structures? Or did things change?

So it sounds like we pretty much have everything that I want
in terms of functionality.

Are the other functions like stan() built on top of these,
or implemented independently?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Ideas for RStan
parts:
Linguistic aside: most nouns can be verbed. And the "-ing"
forms are a mess, because they act as present participle verbs
and gerundive nouns (e.g., "John was running" vs. "The running of
the race"). So it's definitely not clear cut.

Then there are constructors, which are function-like but
usually named after nouns.

Anyway, it's not a very strong convention anywhere.

- Bob

Hi—I think it’s fine to have various primitive functions as long as the wrappers do what I need.  I need a stan() function that has what Bob calls make-like behavior and is set by default to save the compiled models in the working directory, similarly a stan_optimize() function (or some other name) that does the same thing with optimization and returns an object from which we can extract the mode, the second-derivative matrix, and various other things.  Also we need various verbose options including complete silence as an option.  It’s fine with me if this is all done by calling the basic functions; indeed, I think this will make the documentation that much clearer.
A

On Jun 7, 2014, at 12:14 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On Jun 6, 2014, at 9:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Hi, Bob.  I put it on stan-dev because non R-users might have thoughts too.

Thanks.

At some point we can talk about how best to write a spec.  My main thought is to switch to Sebastian's function (or something like it), also to clean up the stan-optimize call and a few other things.

I don't think we need a formal spec process --- just
a simple functional spec consisting of the documentation for 
the functions you want to see implemented including examples.
Then, the folks who know R can turn it into a technical spec
that explains how to implement it, but I don't think we
need to formalize a technical spec if the functional spec is solid.

I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
of examples.  Here's what I would like to see for compilation:

 model <- compile("foo.stan");

for fitting:

 mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
 mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);

and for saving and reloading:

 save_model(model=, file=);
 model <- load_model(file=);

To turn this into a functional spec we can work from, 
we have to add descriptions of

 * the rest of the arguments

 * types for each argument

 * return type

 * constraints on legal calling patterns --- the spec has to
   say exactly what arguments require other arguments or disallow
   other arguments, and what sets of legal values there are (this
   is the killer that most R functions don't even bother with, making
   them very difficult to learn)

 * types of errors that get thrown under what conditions

 * description of what the function does

 * examples of how the function is used in practice

I don't really underestand R well enough to talk about the 
types myself or error handling, other than in broad generalities. 

You'll see that using primitive functions will make writing
this spec much easier, which will in turn make development and
testing much easier.  It should also make it easier to play around
with higher-level functions that may be more changeable and less
well supported (due to prohibitive combinatorics of testing and doc).

- Bob

A

On Jun 5, 2014, at 10:24 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

1.  Do you have a spec for how you think it should be
rewritten to be less clunky?

2.  Should we move this discussion to stan-dev, or perhaps
start an rstan-dev mailing list?  

- Bob

On Jun 5, 2014, at 1:20 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Hi all.  Maybe next week when we've finished this current grant application, we can talk about fixing up Rstan.  Right now, running stan from R is clunky, and doing mle requires a ton of function calls.  So I'd like to put some new functions in Rstan (and clean up the functions we have) so this can all be done.  Thx
A

On May 23, 2014, at 6:58 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

OK, 2 functions is fine.  Maybe stan() and stan_optimize()?  Or optimize_stan()?  What do you think?
A
On May 23, 2014, at 6:35 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On May 23, 2014, at 4:09 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Hi all.  What's most important to me is that the workhorse stan() function have make-like behavior.  I _don't_ want to have to call stan() one way the first time (passing it the file name) and another way a later time (passing it the R object name).

Perhaps given what you two say, we should have the three primitive functions as you define them, and then have one or more wrappers of the sort that I like.  

That would make me happier.

The wrappers would include the following:

- stan() with make-like behavior
- the same thing for stan_optimize (or maybe that should just be stan() with optimize=TRUE; I don't feel strongly about this)

I feel pretty strongly that these should not be merged
into a single command.

Optimization and sampling take different parameters and
produce different output data structures.  Combining them
then becomes this big conditional exercise.

Compare:

c foo(a,b)
d bar(e,f);

with

[c OR d] foo_bar(a, b, e, f);

+ doc that if a or b is defined then return is c and 
 e and f can't be and vice-versa

Let's not be foo_bar!

- Bob

That's still not quite precise enough to be a spec.

I take it by make-like behavior here, you want to recompile
if the time stamp of the model file is later than that of
the compiled version.

But what do you do if the model's given as a string, which
seems to be popular among our R users. Personally, I'd try
to discourage that behavior because it's a pain for us
to debug when everything's tied up in R --- I believe most of our
C++ developers don't ever use R. But then I don't like
Sweave (or whatever it's called now) for the same reason.

Andrew --- could you go through ALL the other arguments
to stan() and make sure they're what you want?

I would very much like to avoid continually changing our
functions. Let's try to get it as close to right in a single
change.

- Bob

> to discourage that behavior because it's a pain for us
> to debug when everything's tied up in R --- I believe most of our
> C++ developers don't ever use R. But then I don't like
> Sweave (or whatever it's called now) for the same reason.
>
> Andrew --- could you go through ALL the other arguments
> to stan() and make sure they're what you want?
>
> I would very much like to avoid continually changing our
> functions. Let's try to get it as close to right in a single
> change.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 11, 2014, at 5:36 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>

>> Hi--I think it's fine to have various primitive functions as long as the wrappers do what I need. I need a stan() function that has what Bob calls make-like behavior and is set by default to save the compiled models in the working directory, similarly a stan_optimize() function (or some other name) that does the same thing with optimization and returns an object from which we can extract the mode, the second-derivative matrix, and various other things. Also we need various verbose options including complete silence as an option. It's fine with me if this is all done by calling the basic functions; indeed, I think this will make the documentation that much clearer.

>> A
>>
>> On Jun 7, 2014, at 12:14 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>>> On Jun 6, 2014, at 9:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>
>>>> Hi, Bob. I put it on stan-dev because non R-users might have thoughts too.
>>>
>>> Thanks.
>>>
>>>> At some point we can talk about how best to write a spec. My main thought is to switch to Sebastian's function (or something like it), also to clean up the stan-optimize call and a few other things.
>>>
>>> I don't think we need a formal spec process --- just
>>> a simple functional spec consisting of the documentation for
>>> the functions you want to see implemented including examples.
>>> Then, the folks who know R can turn it into a technical spec
>>> that explains how to implement it, but I don't think we
>>> need to formalize a technical spec if the functional spec is solid.
>>>
>>> I'll go first with a really informal functional spec just consisting
>>> of examples. Here's what I would like to see for compilation:
>>>
>>> model <- compile("foo.stan");
>>>
>>> for fitting:
>>>
>>> mle_fit <- optimize(model=, data=, ...);
>>> mcmc_fit <- stan(model=, data=, ...);
>>>
>>> and for saving and reloading:
>>>
>>> save_model(model=, file=);
>>> model <- load_model(file=);
>>>
>>> To turn this into a functional spec we can work from,
>>> we have to add descriptions of
>>>
>>> * the rest of the arguments
>>>
>>> * types for each argument
>>>
>>> * return type
>>>
>>> * constraints on legal calling patterns --- the spec has to
>>> say exactly what arguments require other arguments or disallow
>>> other arguments, and what sets of legal values there are (this
>>> is the killer that most R functions don't even bother with, making
>>> them very difficult to learn)
>>>
>>> * types of errors that get thrown under what conditions
>>>
>>> * description of what the function does
>>>
>>> * examples of how the function is used in practice
>>>
>>> I don't really underestand R well enough to talk about the
>>> types myself or error handling, other than in broad generalities.
>>>
>>> You'll see that using primitive functions will make writing
>>> this spec much easier, which will in turn make development and
>>> testing much easier. It should also make it easier to play around
>>> with higher-level functions that may be more changeable and less
>>> well supported (due to prohibitive combinatorics of testing and doc).
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>

>>>>>>>>>

Bob,

You mean saving in an external .stan file or in R's workspace?

For Julia I've been thinking about the .stan file approach, but with similar reservations as being raised in this thread.

At least in that approach I have the option to compare the "model as a string" with the contents of the .stan file and if changed, update the file and thus trigger make.

Inside the Julia code I have not decided yet to store the model as a string or use a macro (or a macro for each model section). I'm first focusing on the command input and output structures in Julia.
